cards.heading: The problem
cards.body: Hosts have a single default gateway. If that router fails, they lose everything off their subnet, even when a second router is right there. A first hop redundancy protocol (FHRP) lets two or more routers share a virtual IP and virtual MAC that hosts use as their gateway.

cards.heading: HSRP active and standby
cards.body: HSRP (Cisco) elects one active router, which answers for the virtual IP and MAC, and one standby router ready to take over. Hellos go every 3 seconds; the standby takes over if it hears nothing for 10 (hold time). Hosts notice nothing: the gateway's IP and MAC stay the same.
cards.example:
Virtual IP 10.1.1.1 / 0000.0c07.ac01
   R1 .2 (active)        R2 .3 (standby)
          \                /
               [SW1]
             PCs: gateway 10.1.1.1

cards.heading: Election
cards.body: Highest priority wins (default 100, range 0-255). If priorities tie, the highest interface IP wins. Priority ranges 0-255 with a default of 100.
cards.example:
interface g0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.2 255.255.255.0
 standby 1 ip 10.1.1.1
 standby 1 priority 110

cards.heading: Preempt
cards.body: HSRP doesn't take the active role from a working active router, even if a router with a higher priority joins later, unless that router has 'standby 1 preempt'. Without preempt, whoever came up first stays active.

cards.heading: Interface tracking
cards.body: If the active router's uplink fails, it still answers hosts but can't forward their traffic anywhere useful. Tracking lowers its priority when the tracked interface goes down, so a peer with preempt takes over. The decrement must push it below the peer.

cards.heading: Virtual MACs
cards.body: HSRPv1 uses 0000.0c07.acXX and HSRPv2 0000.0c9f.fXXX, where X is the group number in hex. HSRPv2 supports groups 0-4095 and IPv6.

cards.heading: VRRP and GLBP
cards.body: VRRP is the open standard (RFC 5798): master and backup routers, preempt on by default, and the virtual IP may be a real router's address. GLBP (Cisco) load-balances: one active virtual gateway (AVG) hands out different virtual MACs so several forwarders (AVFs) share the traffic. If the VRRP virtual IP is one router's real address, that address owner gets priority 255 and is always master; HSRP needs a separate virtual address. In GLBP the AVG answers ARP for the virtual IP with the MACs of up to four AVFs, spreading hosts across them. HSRP and GLBP are Cisco-proprietary; VRRP is the open standard.

cards.heading: HSRP states, versions and addresses
cards.body: A group has one active and one standby router; any others wait in the Listen state and only speak up if the active or standby fails. Only the active router forwards for the virtual IP, so sharing load needs several groups or GLBP. When hosts ARP for the virtual IP, the reply carries the group's virtual MAC; that MAC moves with the active role, so after a failover hosts keep the same gateway MAC and don't need to ARP again. 'show standby brief' lists each group's priority, P for preempt, state, active and standby routers and virtual IP.
cards.example:
HSRPv1  groups 0-255   hellos to 224.0.0.2    MAC 0000.0c07.acXX
HSRPv2  groups 0-4095  hellos to 224.0.0.102  MAC 0000.0c9f.fXXX  (IPv6 too)
VRRP    hellos to 224.0.0.18                   MAC 0000.5e00.01XX
GLBP    MAC 0007.b4XX.XXYY
